query: For structural materials intended for fusion plasma-facing components, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis explains what governs high-temperature plastic strain and toughness, and why? Specify a controlled comparison that would isolate the hypothesized cause, the observations predicted relative to an unperturbed baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, the prior evidence supporting it, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In fusion-relevant tungsten-based plasma-facing alloys, a controlled thermal pre-aging treatment that increases grain boundary precipitate density will impede dislocation climb and grain boundary sliding, thereby reducing high-temperature plastic strain and enhancing toughness relative to the as-manufactured state.
generation.material_initial_state: As-manufactured tungsten-based alloy with a random, baseline grain boundary precipitate distribution.
generation.intervention: Application of a targeted thermal pre-aging treatment to engineer an increased, uniformly dispersed, and coherent precipitate network specifically at grain boundaries while maintaining constant alloy composition.
generation.conditions: High-temperature mechanical testing under fusion-relevant conditions (e.g., temperatures above 700°C) in an unirradiated environment.
generation.structural_mediator: Grain boundary precipitate density and coherence.
generation.mechanism: Enhanced precipitate density at grain boundaries acts as physical barriers to dislocation climb and limits grain boundary sliding, resulting in decreased plastic deformation and improved toughness at high temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared with unaged samples, the pre-aged alloys will exhibit reduced plastic strain (increased yield strength and improved creep resistance) and higher fracture toughness due to the controlled precipitate network.
generation.baseline: Unaged tungsten-based alloy with its native, less optimized precipitate distribution.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold for tungsten-based plasma-facing alloys under high-temperature conditions typical of fusion reactors, provided that the precipitate structure remains coherent and does not undergo excessive coarsening or destabilization.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative relationship between precipitate density and the extent of dislocation inhibition is not fully defined; additionally, the stability of the engineered precipitates under prolonged thermal exposure may vary with specific alloy microchemistry.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of tungsten-based alloys with identical compositions: one set receives a deliberate thermal pre-aging treatment to increase grain boundary precipitate density, while the control set remains in its as-manufactured state. Subject both sets to high-temperature tensile and creep tests under identical conditions.
measurements: Quantitative analysis of grain boundary precipitate density and morphology (using TEM/SEM)
High-temperature yield strength and creep rate measurements
Fracture toughness or impact testing to assess ductility and toughness
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pre-aged samples do not demonstrate a statistically significant reduction in plastic strain and an increase in toughness relative to the control, or if mechanical properties deteriorate unexpectedly, the hypothesis is falsified.

Options for sustainable clean energy include advanced power generation systems that have the potential to drastically reduce the emission of greenhouse gases. These advanced systems are often required to operate under harsh conditions to optimize efficiency, which poses several challenges for the available materials. An example of advanced power system is one that is associated with fusion energy [1] . Beyond traditional fission-based systems, fusion reactors not only promise nearly unlimited clean energy, but also avoid the generation of long-life radioactive waste produced in fission devices. Abstract This article presents the high temperature tensile and creep behaviors of a novel high entropy alloy (HEA). The microstructure of this HEA resembles that of advanced superalloys with a high entropy FCC matrix and L1 2 ordered precipitates, so it is also named as “high entropy superalloy (HESA)”. The tensile yield strengths of HESA surpass those of the reported HEAs from room temperature to elevated temperatures; furthermore, its creep resistance at 982 °C can be compared to those of some Ni-based superalloys. Analysis on experimental results indicate that HESA could be strengthened by the low stacking-fault energy of the matrix, high anti-phase boundary energy of the strengthening precipitate, and thermally stable microstructure. Positive misfit between FCC matrix and precipitate has yielded parallel raft microstructure during creep at 982 °C, and the creep curves of HESA were dominated by tertiary creep behavior. To the best of authors’ knowledge, this article is the first to present the elevated temperature tensile creep study on full scale specimens of a high entropy alloy, and the potential of HESA for high temperature structural application is discussed.

While the AlCoFeNi high entropy alloy exhibits a single ordered B2 phase at high temperature, both the substitution of ferromagnetic Co with antiferromagnetic Cr, and lower annealing temperatures lead to a tendency for this system to decompose into a two-phase mixture of ordered B2 and disordered BCC solid solution. The length scale of this decomposition is determined by the combination of composition and annealing temperature, as demonstrated in this investigation by comparing and contrasting AlCoFeNi with the AlCo 0.5 Cr 0.5 FeNi alloy. The resulting phase stability has been rationalized based on solution thermodynamic predictions. Additionally, it is shown that replacement of Co by Cr in the AlCoFeNi alloy resulted in a substantial reduction in saturation magnetization and increase in coercivity. The microhardness is also strongly influenced by the composition and the length scale of B2 + BCC decomposition in these high entropy alloys.

In this study, bulk samples of a CrMoNbWV high-entropy alloy (HEA) were obtained for the first time by spark plasma sintering (SPS) of mechanically alloyed (MA) powders at 1200 °C, 1300 °C, and 1400 °C. Microstructure evolution, phase formation as well as wear and corrosion behavior were investigated. The MA powders’ phase composition was found to be represented by body-centered-cubic (BCC) solid solution. The solid solution partially decomposed to Laves phases under the sintering, such as Cr 2 Nb and (Fe, Cr)Nb, and NbVO 4 -VO oxides mixture. The temperature increase to 1400 °C led to a grain coarsening of the BCC phase and decreased the Laves phase content accompanied by precipitation at the grain boundaries. The sintered samples showed high hardness and compressive strength (2700–2800 MPa) at room temperature. The wear tests demonstrated excellent results in comparison to conventional wear-resistant composites. The obtained samples also exhibited high corrosion resistance under electrochemical tests in H 2 SO 4 solution. frame.system: Structural materials (e.g., tungsten-based alloys or other plasma‐facing alloys) in their as‐manufactured or thermally pre‐aged microstructural state intended for use as plasma‐facing components in fusion reactors.
frame.goal: Identify a single, testable mechanistic hypothesis that explains the governing mechanism behind high-temperature plastic strain and toughness, with a focus on correlating specific microstructural features (such as dislocation mobility, grain boundary behavior, or second-phase precipitate evolution) to mechanical response at fusion-relevant temperatures.
frame.limitation: Lack of a unified, mechanistic explanation that isolates and directly tests the dominant microstructural process controlling high-temperature plastic deformation and toughness, particularly given the complex thermal, irradiation, and stress conditions in fusion environments.

decision.trend: Early studies in high‐entropy and refractory alloys used empirical correlations and high‐strain simulations to observe how various microstructural features (e.g., clustering‐to‐ordering transitions, dislocation dynamics, dynamic precipitate formation) correlated with mechanical responses under high temperatures. Initial work (e.g., PMC4976365, PMC5578249) demonstrated that deformation mode and processing history affect dislocation configurations and secondary phase evolution. Later work (PMC7512559, PMC7514651) increasingly focused on identifying specific deformation mechanisms such as stress-assisted dislocation climb and dynamic recrystallization, while some tungsten-based systems (PMC6397024) revealed the role of fine precipitates and segregation at grain boundaries. However, even with advanced characterization (PMC11206460) the field has not isolated a singular, causal microstructural lever that directly controls high-temperature plastic strain and toughness in fusion‐relevant plasma–facing alloys.
decision.unsolved: The dominant microstructural process remains ambiguous. It is unclear whether high-temperature plastic strain and toughness are chiefly governed by dislocation climb controlled by localized grain boundary diffusion, by precipitate pinning that limits dislocation motion, or by a synergy involving grain boundary sliding. In fusion environments—with extreme thermal gradients and irradiation—the interplay between precipitate stability, dislocation mobility, and grain boundary behavior has not been decoupled in a controlled fashion, leaving a gap in a single, testable mechanistic explanation.
decision.lever: engineer a controlled variation of grain boundary precipitate density through targeted thermal pre-aging while maintaining constant alloy composition
decision.why: This approach isolates the effect of a key microstructural parameter—precipitate density at grain boundaries—on dislocation climb and grain boundary sliding under fusion-relevant high-temperature conditions. Based on the trend, earlier work has identified complex, simultaneous contributions from microstructural evolutions without a definitive causal lever. By holding composition constant and varying only the precipitate network (via controlled pre-aging), the experiment should directly test the hypothesis that an optimally dispersed and coherent precipitate structure moderates dislocation mobility (and hence plastic strain) while enhancing toughness relative to an unperturbed baseline. A lack of the predicted improvements under these controlled conditions would falsify the hypothesis.
